c1.story:
Most industries have thousands of customers. Indian defence has, for practical purposes, one: the Ministry of Defence, buying for the army, the navy and the air force. That single fact shapes everything about the business, from how orders arrive to why the stocks swing the way they do.

Within that one-customer world, there are four very different ways to make money.

The first door belongs to the state-owned primes. Hindustan Aeronautics builds fighters, trainers and helicopters. Bharat Electronics builds radars, communication networks and the electronics of air-defence systems. Bharat Dynamics builds missiles. They design, integrate and deliver whole platforms on contracts that run for years, and the ministry pays a large share upfront as advances. They are, in effect, the government's own factories, and the government wants them to prosper.

The second door is the shipyards: Mazagon Dock in Mumbai, Cochin Shipyard, Garden Reach in Kolkata, and Swan Defence, the old Pipavav yard revived after an insolvency process. They build destroyers, frigates, submarines and patrol vessels, each over five to ten years, on fixed-price contracts with big advances. Cochin Shipyard built INS Vikrant, India's first home-built aircraft carrier. The visibility is the longest in the market; the conversion into revenue is the slowest.

The primes have the orders, the shipyards have the patience, and the private names have the growth.

The third door is the private electronics and sub-system makers: Data Patterns, Apollo Micro Systems, Paras Defence, Krishna Defence. They design and build the radar modules, missile electronics and optics that go inside the primes' platforms. Their order books are small enough that a single contract can double or halve a year.

The fourth door looks outward. Precision engineering firms machine engine parts, airframe pieces and tooling for global aircraft makers. For them, an Airbus production rate matters more than an Indian budget speech.

The same headline, say a big fighter approval, means a decade of revenue for the prime, a possible sub-system order for the private supplier a year later, and almost nothing for the aerospace parts maker.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you the contract shape: multi-year platform contracts with advances, multi-year ship contracts with advances, supplier orders from the primes and labs, or parts orders from global aircraft makers.
  • The tickers are the listed names behind each door. Click one for its stock page. Notice the split: the first two doors are almost all government-owned; the last two are private.
  • The profit bar tells you how much of the value the company keeps. State-owned primes sit at the high end. That surprises people, since their only customer is all-powerful, but the customer wants these factories strong, contracts are often priced on cost plus a margin, and the primes face no domestic rival on platforms. Shipyards sit in the middle, because fixed prices and long builds expose them to cost slips. Private electronics and aerospace parts also sit in the middle: real skills, but squeezed by the primes or by global buyers above them.
  • The last line is the bet. For the shipyards it hides a detail worth knowing: finishing a ship early can earn an incentive, finishing late costs penalties, so the margin swings on the calendar.

Below the tiles, the analogy of the government's kitchen, the banquet hall, the spice supplier and the cutlery maker gives you the four in one breath.

The so-what line is the practical rule: the primes have the orders and the cash, the shipyards the longest visibility and slowest conversion, the private names the growth and the lumpiness. Size a position accordingly.

c2.story:
A fighter rolling out of HAL's Bengaluru hangar looks unmistakably Indian. Follow its parts back through the kitchen, though, and the story gets more international with every step.

Station one is research and design. DRDO, the government's defence research organisation, and the design bureaus inside HAL and BEL draw the aircraft, the missile or the radar. But some things India still cannot design at home, and the most important is the jet engine. The Tejas runs on an American GE engine. Licensed designs from Russia, France and Israel fill other gaps. This is where the foreign original equipment makers stand.

Station two is materials and components: special steels, titanium, composites, chips, optics and missile seekers. Midhani, the state alloy maker, supplies some metals; Paras makes optics; Apollo and Data Patterns build electronics. But much of the sensor and chip content still arrives from Israel, the US and Europe.

Station three is sub-systems, where components become radar modules, missile guidance units, sonar, hull blocks and machined engine parts. This is where India's private defence ecosystem lives: listed suppliers plus hundreds of small vendors around Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune.

A fighter stamped Made in India can still be waiting for a box from Ohio.

Station four is platform integration. HAL, BEL, BDL and the shipyards assemble everything into a fighter, a frigate, a missile battery or a radar network, with the government's quality agencies inspecting at every step. Station five is delivery, decades of upkeep, and increasingly exports, to buyers in Southeast Asia, Africa and the Gulf.

Here is the uncomfortable truth the kitchen reveals. India has largely nationalised the last two stations: integration and delivery are firmly Indian. The first two stations, where the engine and the sensor come from, are where both the profit and the delay originate. When GE's engine deliveries for the Tejas slipped, HAL had airframes ready and nothing to put in them. Revenue waited a year on one supplier's production line.
c2.read:
Five station boxes on top, a band row underneath. Read the boxes left to right.

The five boxes run from design on the left to delivery and export on the right. Under each name you get what happens there and who stands there. As you move right, the names shift from DRDO and foreign engine makers, to alloy and electronics suppliers, to private sub-system makers, to the primes and yards, and finally to the armed forces and export customers.

The band row is unusual on this card. Station one is coloured as the rival band, DRDO and foreign OEMs. That is the visual statement that the most critical knowledge, especially engines, still sits outside listed India. Station two is imports and Midhani. Listed India holds stations three and four, sub-systems and integration. Station five belongs to the customer, the armed forces.

So listed defence is a middle-of-the-chain business, just as in many industries, but with a twist: its supplier at station one is often its own government lab, or a foreign company whose government controls export licences.

Read the geography note next. Bengaluru for aerospace, Hyderabad for missiles and electronics, and the shipyards on both coasts. Its last line is the one to remember: the foreign content hides in the engines and sensors.

Use the diagram as a delay tracer. A late engine at station one becomes an undelivered fighter at station four. A sensor export licence held up abroad at station two becomes a missile battery waiting for its seeker. The so-what line sums it up: India has nationalised the last two stations, and both the profit and the delay come from the first two.

c3.story:
In most industries, demand is the sum of millions of choices. In Indian defence, it is the sum of a few committee meetings. Three services and one ministry make almost every buying decision, which means demand is a policy choice, not a market outcome. It can be accelerated by a border clash or frozen by a scandal.

The air force is the biggest-ticket buyer and the one with the most visible problem: too few fighter squadrons as old Soviet-era aircraft retire. That gap is why HAL signed for a large batch of upgraded Tejas fighters in 2021 and a second, bigger batch in September 2025. But the air force's demand runs through a supply bottleneck: imported engines decide how fast those fighters actually arrive.

The navy buys on the longest horizon of all. Its fleet plan, sharpened by Chinese naval activity in the Indian Ocean, keeps destroyers, frigates and submarines flowing to Mazagon Dock, Garden Reach and Cochin Shipyard for a decade at a time. Mazagon built the Scorpene-class submarines with France's Naval Group, and the navy's carrier-borne fighter deal for French Rafales, signed in 2025, adds another layer of demand.

The army is the most event-driven. Border tension with China and Pakistan triggers emergency procurement powers, and artillery, air-defence missiles, radios, drones and night vision are bought quickly. Operation Sindoor in May 2025 was a live demonstration: Indian-made missiles and air defence, including the Akash system built by BEL and BDL, performed in combat, and emergency orders followed.

A border clash moves the stocks for a month. A fleet plan moves the earnings for a decade.

Then come the customers who help solve the one-customer problem. Exports have hit records, led by deals such as the Philippines' purchase of BrahMos missiles in 2022. ISRO and newly private space companies buy launch structures and satellite electronics. And global aerospace majors buy machined parts from Indian suppliers as they diversify away from China. None of these is yet as large as the home market, but each one makes a company less dependent on a single ministry's calendar.
c3.read:
Seven tiles, one per customer. Each has three lines.

  • The name: the buyer.
  • What it buys: tells you which door benefits. Fighters and helicopters point to HAL; ships and sonar to the yards and BEL; missiles to BDL; parts to the aerospace door.
  • What moves it: your watch list. Squadron shortfalls and engine deliveries for the air force; the fleet plan and Chinese naval activity for the navy; border tension for the army; government-to-government deals for exports; launch cadence for space; Airbus and Boeing production rates for the global majors.

Sort the tiles into two groups. The first four, the three services and the paramilitary, are the home budget. They are huge but they share one wallet and one approval process. The last three, export customers, space and global aerospace, are the diversifiers. They are smaller, but they follow different clocks.

Then link each to a door. A prime selling mostly to the air force is tied to engine deliveries. A shipyard is tied to the navy's fleet plan and its own dock capacity. A private electronics name can sit behind several tiles at once, which is one reason its lumpiness can smooth out over time. An aerospace parts maker barely touches the first four tiles at all.

The so-what under the grid warns that a single committee meeting can accelerate or freeze demand. So the best use of this grid is as a map of whose decisions to follow: each tile's moves-with line names the decision-maker or event that will show up in orders a year later.

c4.story:
Picture a caterer with one extremely wealthy client. The client pays half the bill before the wedding. The caterer puts that money in a fixed deposit, earns interest on it, and cooks at a measured pace. The risk is not that the client leaves; there is nowhere else to go. The risk is that the imported oven arrives late. That, roughly, is the economics of an Indian defence prime.

Look at the raw-material line first. A prime spends about half its revenue on materials, components and imported kits. Here is the subtle point: an imported kit carries almost no margin for the prime. If HAL assembles a licensed design from foreign kits, it earns an integration fee. If it designs and sources the parts at home, it keeps far more. Rising indigenous content is not only a patriotic slogan; it is a margin lever.

The shipyards have a heavier raw-material bill, with steel, engines, weapons and sensors bought in, and fixed-price contracts that run for years. So their margins are thinner, and they swing on the calendar. Finish a ship early and you may earn an incentive; finish late and liquidated damages, contractual penalties for delay, eat into profit.

Strip out the interest on the customer's own money, and you see what the factory really earns.

Now the line that flatters everyone. The forces pay large advances, and those advances sit on the balance sheet as cash. Interest on that cash flows into other income. For a shipyard, it can be a fifth of profit. That is real money, but it is treasury income, not manufacturing skill, and it will shrink if rates fall or advances are consumed.

Depreciation and interest barely matter. The PSU factories are old and largely written down, and almost every listed name is debt-free. Capex matters only when it unlocks the order book: a new Tejas production line at HAL, a new dry dock at a yard. And working capital is a tale of two doors: negative for shipyards sitting on advances, painfully positive for private suppliers waiting on the primes to pay.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: on the left a state-owned platform prime, on the right a shipyard.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar, materials, components and imported kits, takes roughly half of a prime's sales and about seven tenths of a shipyard's. That gap is design content: a prime that designs more keeps more.
  • The opex bar, people, testing, power and overheads, is bigger at the prime, roughly a quarter of sales, because design engineers and flight testing are expensive.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is a barely visible sliver in both. Old factories, no debt.
  • The last bar is what is left. The prime keeps about a fifth of sales; the shipyard about half that.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the amount. And note one thing the bars do not show: other income from advances, which sits below them and makes reported profit look better still.

The list below marks which lines matter. Order book and inflow, revenue conversion of the book, gross margin with indigenous content, and other income from advances all get a yes. Working capital, capex and liquidated damages get a sometimes, each with a door-specific reason. Depreciation and interest get a no.

Notice that other income is a yes here, which is rare. In most industries on this page it is noise. In defence it can be a fifth of a shipyard's profit, which is why the so-what line tells you to strip it out to see what the factories actually earn.

c5.story:
Defence does not have a market cycle in the usual sense. Nobody's prices crash because of a glut of frigates. It has a policy cycle: periods when the government wants to buy, buys at home and decides quickly, and periods when it does none of those things.

The last boom came after Kargil. From 2004 to 2010, modernisation money flowed, large import deals were signed and the PSU primes grew fat on licensed production of foreign designs. Then came the brake. Around 2010 to 2012, the VVIP helicopter bribery scandal and a run of blacklisted vendors made the ministry deeply cautious. Files piled up in committees.

The bust from 2013 to 2018 was long and dull. Procurement froze. The marquee fighter tender for over a hundred aircraft collapsed into a small off-the-shelf purchase of Rafales. HAL listed in 2018 into a cold market and its shares slipped below the issue price. By 2019, the aircraft prime was borrowing to pay salaries while it waited for the ministry to clear its dues.

Then two events reset the policy. The Balakot strikes in 2019 exposed the squadron gap. The Galwan clash with China in 2020 changed the politics entirely: the first list of weapons that could no longer be imported was published, foreign ownership limits were raised, and the procurement manual was rewritten to rank Indian design first.

Galwan did for Indian defence stocks what no budget speech ever had: it made buying Indian a strategic necessity.

The boom that followed was spectacular. Big Tejas orders, record exports, the first home-built carrier commissioned, private suppliers listing and re-rating. In 2024 order placement slowed into the election, valuations were extreme and the stocks corrected sharply even as order books stayed full. Then Operation Sindoor in May 2025 proved Indian-made missiles in combat, emergency orders followed, a second Tejas batch and carrier-borne Rafales were cleared, and the stocks rallied back.

Today the constraint is not demand. It is engines, docks and delivery.
c5.read:
Three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. Under each arc sit the years of the last policy cycle: boom from 2004 to 2010, peak around 2010 to 2012, bust from 2013 to 2018, bottom in 2019 and 2020. The arrow points into the boom arc, labelled boom, execution-paced: record order books, deliveries lag engines. Hover an arc to read what defined that phase.

The timeline from 2019 is colour-coded. 2019 is a bust year. 2020 is neutral, the hinge year when Galwan reset policy. Then boom entries for 2021 to 2023, a neutral 2024 for the election-year correction, boom again in 2025 after Operation Sindoor, and the now entry for 2026, where order books stand at several years of sales.

The four hands are what you watch.

  • Defence capital budget growth: rising in the low teens, arrow up. More approvals can become contracts.
  • Order book to sales at the primes: several years, arrow up. Good only if execution keeps pace.
  • Engine and import deliveries: slipping, arrow down. This is the one hand pointing the wrong way, and it is the most important: late engines mean fighters built but not delivered.
  • Export order wins: rising, arrow up. Proof of competitiveness and a loosening of the one-customer problem.

Three hands up on demand, one down on supply. That is what an execution-paced boom looks like. The so-what states the consequence: revenue, not orders, is the surprise variable, and a stock can fall on a record order book if deliveries slip.

c6.story:
Most industries on this page are moved by prices: copper, crude, interest rates. Defence is moved by decisions. Three of them carry the heaviest weight, and none has a price chart.

The first is the defence capital budget, the slice of defence spending that buys new equipment rather than paying salaries and pensions. It is the money available to sign and pay for contracts. A rise this year shows up as orders and advances next year. The second is border tension. Conflict pulls orders forward through emergency procurement and stiffens political will for big programmes. The third, and the most important for listed companies, is the share of procurement bought at home. A rupee spent on an imported fighter does nothing for HAL; a rupee shifted onto a positive indigenisation list flows straight to Indian order books.

Conflict moves the stocks for a month. The budget and the share bought at home move the earnings for a decade.

Then come the dials that cost money. A weaker rupee raises the cost of imported engines, sensors and kits on contracts priced in rupees. Western export controls and delivery schedules decide when engines and sensors arrive; tighter controls, or simply a busy American factory, delay fighters and ships. And fiscal space matters because a stretched government finds it easier to delay capital spending, or payments to the primes, than to cut salaries.

A few dials are double-edged. Global defence spending is rising, which opens export markets for Indian missiles and radars but also tightens the supply of the very engines and parts India needs. Crude oil hurts the Indian budget but swells the wallets of Gulf export customers.

And one dial runs the opposite way from most industries: higher interest rates help. Because the primes and yards sit on large customer advances in cash, higher rates lift their other income. It is a small effect, but it shows how unusual this industry's balance sheets are.
c6.read:
One row per dial. Read across: the dial, its channel, what a rise does, its weight and today's reading.

  • Channel: the route into profits, from the money available to sign contracts to the interest earned on advances.
  • A rise does: green up arrows on the capital budget, border tension, the share bought at home and, unusually, interest rates. Red down arrows on the rupee, Western export controls, fiscal space and steel. Diamonds on global defence spending and crude.
  • Weight: three rows carry three dots, the most of any industry here: capital budget, border tension and share bought at home. That trio is the whole thesis.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track. Look closely at which ones do: the rupee, a bond proxy for fiscal space, exports, the money-market rate, steel output and crude. Two of the three heaviest dials, the capital budget and the share bought at home, have no live series at all and show a dash; border tension is proxied by the market's volatility index, a rough stand-in. In other words, the dials that matter most for defence are read from budget documents and policy announcements, not from a price screen.

How to use it: after each Union budget, check the capital line and any new indigenisation list. Those two readings will tell you more about the next few years than any quarterly result. Then glance at the red rows to see whether engines and fiscal pressure are slowing delivery and payment.

The so-what line puts it plainly: track the defence capital budget and the share bought at home.

c7.story:
Indian defence has an odd problem for a booming industry. Demand is not the constraint. The government has signed, the order books are full, and the stocks have priced it in. What limits growth is how fast the factories and their foreign suppliers can actually deliver.

The biggest bottleneck is the engine. India does not make a fighter engine. Marine gas turbines and many helicopter engines are imported too. When GE's deliveries of Tejas engines slipped, HAL's fighter line slowed to a crawl, and with it the revenue that analysts had pencilled in. GE and HAL agreed in 2023 to produce a more powerful GE engine in India, but a truly home-grown fighter engine remains years away.

Sensors and chips follow the same pattern. Seekers, infrared sensors and radar chips come from Israel, the US and Europe. A diplomatic chill or a supplier's own backlog upstream becomes a delivery slip downstream.

India has the order books of a superpower and the engine supply of a customer.

Then the factories themselves. When order books hit several years of sales, the production line becomes the limit. HAL has added a production line for the Tejas, but each line takes years and skilled hands to stand up. Shipyards face the physical version: each yard has a fixed number of docks and slipways, and a delayed launch blocks the next keel from being laid.

The customer brings its own frictions. The ministry decides on its own clock; a programme can take years to move from approval to signed contract, and a new minister can reset it. When its budget runs short, it has paid the primes late, which is how HAL ended up borrowing for salaries in 2019. And procurement scandals, from Bofors in the 1980s to the helicopter deal a generation later, can blacklist vendors and freeze programmes for years.

Finally, a market bottleneck: retail money arrives in waves. The stocks have swung by half on sentiment while order books barely moved, which is both a risk and an opportunity.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck: what it is, why it bites, and a severity label.

  • Structural: four rows, engines from abroad, one customer with slow decisions, shipyard capacity and dry docks, and imported sensors and chips. That is a heavy structural load. These do not go away with a good budget; they set the pace of the whole industry.
  • Cyclical: execution at the primes. When order books balloon, factories become the limit; when books normalise, so does this.
  • Recurring: payment delays when the ministry's budget runs short, and procurement scandals. Both have happened before and both freeze activity when they return.
  • Two-sided: valuation and retail crowding. It is the only row about the stock rather than the business. It cuts both ways: crowding inflates prices in a rally and creates bargains in a sell-off.

Now read the so-what line, which pairs the rows in an unusual way. The first and third rows, engines and execution, decide this year's revenue. The second and seventh, slow decisions and scandals, decide whether the next decade of orders arrives on time. So split your attention: a quarterly results watch on engines and execution, and a slower political watch on approvals and probity.

A practical habit: when a defence prime misses revenue estimates, check which row caused it. An engine delay is a timing problem that reverses when shipments resume. A slower approval pipeline is a demand problem that compounds. They look identical in a single quarter and very different over two years.

c8.story:
In defence, the rulebook is not something that happens to the industry. It is the industry. Every order begins as a ministry decision and travels through a procurement manual written by the same ministry.

The starting point is the Defence Acquisition Council, chaired by the defence minister. It approves what to buy, in which category and from whom. An approval is called an acceptance of necessity, and it is the first public sign that a programme is coming. But it is only a first sign. The gap between a council approval and a signed contract, often a year or more of trials, negotiation and cabinet clearance, is the sector's real clock.

The Defence Acquisition Procedure, revised in 2020, is the procurement manual. Its most important feature is a ranking of categories that puts indigenously designed, developed and manufactured equipment at the top. A programme in that category is almost guaranteed to go to an Indian prime with an Indian supply chain.

A positive indigenisation list is the closest thing to a guaranteed order a listed company will ever see.

Then the positive indigenisation lists, first published in August 2020: lists of weapons and components that may no longer be imported after set dates. Each list converts future import spending into domestic orders on a schedule. The government has published several since, covering everything from artillery to small components.

Other rules widen the ecosystem. Foreign investment limits were raised so that global majors can set up joint ventures in India, creating orders for local suppliers. Two defence industrial corridors, in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, offer land and incentives for private manufacturing. Export promotion through government-to-government deals and lines of credit is the only real escape from the one-customer problem.

Underneath it all sit DRDO, whose development timelines become the primes' production timelines, and the quality agencies that certify airworthiness. And at the edge, IN-SPACe and the new space policy are opening launch and satellite work to private companies, a second customer set for electronics and structures makers.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care and its status.

  • Always: three rows, the Ministry of Defence with the Defence Acquisition Council, the Department of Defence Production with the quality agencies, and DRDO. These are the permanent machinery. The council is the one to follow most closely, because every large order starts as one of its approvals.
  • Live: five rows, the Defence Acquisition Procedure, the positive indigenisation lists, foreign investment rules, the defence corridors, and export promotion with lines of credit. These are the policy push that turned the sector around after 2020, and each one is still adding orders.
  • New: one row, IN-SPACe and the space policy. A slow-burn second market rather than a quarter mover.

There are no coming rows, which tells you something. The policy architecture is built. What investors watch now is how fast it is used: how many council approvals convert to contracts, how many new items each indigenisation list adds, how many export licences are cleared.

Read the why column of the first row twice: the approval-to-contract gap is the sector's clock. It links directly to the cross-intelligence card, where council approvals appear as the earliest warning signal of all.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. For defence, look there for council approvals, new lists and signed contracts.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces ask who keeps the money. Apply them to Indian defence and you get a result that looks wrong at first glance: the company with an all-powerful single customer keeps the most.

Start with the state-owned primes. Rivalry is almost absent. No Indian private company can build a fighter or a missile system at scale, and the government channels platform work to its own factories. Entry is practically impossible for the same reason. The buyer, the ministry, has full power over price in theory. In practice it wants its own factories to prosper, often prices contracts on cost plus a margin, and pays advances. A customer who wants you to succeed is a very different thing from a customer who merely can squeeze you.

The primes' weak spot is suppliers. Engines and key sensors come from a handful of foreign makers who set their own schedules. HAL can have the government's full backing and still wait on one American factory. That is the heaviest spoke in their shape.

The primes' customer is their protector. Their supplier is their bottleneck.

Substitution is the other force with bite for the primes. The substitute for a prime's product is an import. The indigenisation lists are steadily closing that route, but it has not vanished: big-ticket items like the Rafale still come from abroad.

Now the private electronics names. They face real rivalry, bidding against each other and against the primes' own in-house units. Their buyer is not the friendly ministry but the primes and the labs above them, who can and do squeeze suppliers on price and payment terms. New private suppliers appear every year as the primes outsource more. In return, their parts face little substitution, and they depend somewhat less on foreign engines.

The net result is the pattern from the first card. The primes keep the most because their customer wants them to. The private names grow faster but keep less, and their fortunes rise and fall with how generously the primes choose to outsource.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: state-owned platform primes and private electronics and sub-systems. The overall picture is interesting. The prime's shape is not uniformly small: it is tiny on rivalry and entrants, then shoots out to the outer ring on suppliers. The private shape is rounder and more even, moderate on every spoke.

Look for the crossings. There are two. On suppliers, the prime reaches further, three against two: foreign engine and sensor makers set the schedule. On substitutes, the prime reaches further again, one and a half against one: the import route is a substitute for its product. Everywhere else, the prime's shape sits inside the private one.

The table gives the scores and reasons.

  • Rivalry: half against two. No domestic rival on platforms.
  • Buyer: two against two and a half. One powerful customer for both, but the private names face the primes above them.
  • Entrants: half against two. Nobody enters platform integration; new suppliers appear yearly.

How to use it: the supplier spoke is the one to watch for primes. If engine co-production at home becomes real, that spoke shrinks and the prime's shape becomes small almost everywhere. For the private names, watch the buyer spoke: if the primes outsource more generously, it shrinks; if they bring work in-house, it grows.

c10.story:
Defence results calls are full of excitement: new platforms, export enquiries, technology partnerships. Underneath, eight numbers tell you whether the factory is keeping up with the hype.

Start with the order book against trailing sales, which tells you how many years of revenue are already visible. A few years is excellent. Beyond a certain point, though, a bigger book stops being good news and starts being a question about execution: can the factory ever deliver all that? Then order inflow for the year, which tells you whether council approvals actually became contracts.

Sales growth is the execution check. A record book with sluggish sales growth means deliveries are slipping, usually for want of engines or dock space. EBITDA margin tells you about design content and pricing on cost-plus contracts; primes, shipyards and private electronics each have their own normal range.

In defence, a bigger order book is good news until it becomes a question.

Now the number that separates a factory from a treasury: other income as a share of profit. Customer advances earn interest, and that interest can make a mediocre manufacturing year look healthy. If a large share of pre-tax profit is other income, you are partly buying a fixed deposit.

Receivable days tell you whether the ministry is paying on time, which it has not always done. Return on capital tells you what the business earns on the money tied up in it, ideally measured excluding the customer's own cash, which otherwise distorts the picture. And capex to depreciation asks whether new production lines and docks are being built to clear the book. A prime with a book worth many years of sales and no new capacity is telling you, quietly, that it will take a decade to deliver.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the metric, what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you: the question to ask of each company.
  • What good looks like: the only column with figures. The EBITDA margin row gives three ranges, for primes, shipyards and private electronics; use the one that matches the door. The order book row has a ceiling as well as a floor: above a certain multiple, execution becomes the question.
  • Today's industry median: from the latest annual filings in our database. Three rows have no median, order book to sales, order inflow and other income as a share of profit, because they come from presentations or need adjusting by hand. Those are the rows where your own homework matters most.

A good reading order: order book and inflow from the investor presentation, then sales growth from the results to judge execution, then other income against pre-tax profit to see how much is treasury, and finally capex to depreciation for whether capacity is being added.

Then compare three things for any company: its own number, the industry median and the good mark. Bear in mind the median blends primes, yards and small private suppliers, so its margin will fall somewhere between the door benchmarks.

One special warning for the ROCE row: a debt-free company sitting on customer advances can show an inflated or distorted return on capital. The tells column says it: measure it excluding customer cash.

c11.story:
Defence is the industry where you can see orders coming furthest ahead, because the government announces its intentions in stages. The trick is knowing how long each stage takes.

The earliest signals speak three quarters ahead. A Defence Acquisition Council approval becomes a signed contract and an advance roughly a year later. A new positive indigenisation list converts future imports into domestic orders from its stated date. Both are public, and both tell you about orders that the results will not show for most of a year.

Two quarters ahead come the Union budget's defence capital outlay, foreign engine makers' delivery guidance, export licence approvals and government-to-government talks, the primes' commentary on outsourcing to private vendors, and Airbus and Boeing production rates for the aerospace parts makers. Of these, engine guidance is the one most investors underweight. It sets when fighters actually get delivered, which sets when HAL books the revenue.

And then the same-quarter signal: border incidents and conflict. Emergency orders land within weeks and the stocks move the same day, as they did around Operation Sindoor in May 2025.

Approvals tell you about demand. Engine deliveries tell you about revenue. Confuse the two and you will be surprised every quarter.

These signals feed a three-sign rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when the capital budget is growing, approvals are turning into signed contracts, and deliveries are keeping pace with the book. Three of three is a clean boom; two is a boom with a delivery problem; one is a policy pause. Today the budget is growing in the low teens, a tick. Approvals are converting in a post-conflict rush, a tick. Deliveries are not keeping pace, with engines slipping, a cross.

That gives the call: a policy-driven boom with a delivery bottleneck. Prefer primes and shipyards with proven execution and visible advances, and treat the private small caps as single-contract bets, sized accordingly. Valuations have swung by half twice in three years, so entry price matters more here than almost anywhere.

The chart places outside signals by how far ahead they speak. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

For defence, the dots lean right. Only one sits at the far left: border incidents and conflict, a same-quarter signal. A large group sits at two quarters: the budget's capital outlay, foreign engine delivery guidance, export licences and talks, primes' outsourcing commentary, and Airbus and Boeing rates. Two dots sit furthest right at three quarters: council approvals and new indigenisation lists. This is an industry that warns early, if you read the right documents.

Use it as a reading order. Each quarter, start at the right: what did the council approve, and did a new list appear? Then the two-quarter cluster: is engine guidance improving, are exports clearing, are the primes outsourcing more? The left-hand dot tells you only what has already happened, often already in the price.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs.

  • Capital budget growing: a tick, low teens.
  • Approvals becoming contracts: a tick, post-conflict rush.
  • Deliveries keeping pace: a cross, engines slipping.

Two of three: a boom with a delivery problem.

Finally, the call box with its points and what would change it. Use the last three as alerts. A procurement scandal or ministerial reset would freeze signings. A fiscal squeeze would flatten the budget or delay payments. And engine deliveries normalising is the upside alert: it would turn the cross into a tick and release a revenue catch-up.
